name: Intralesional steroid / 5-FU for keloids

card.summary: Clinic-delivered injections of a corticosteroid, sometimes with 5-fluorouracil, to flatten raised keloid scars; a standard dermatology procedure with limited comparative evidence.
card.aka: Intralesional triamcinolone, triamcinolone/5-FU combination, keloid injections
card.note: Medical procedure performed by clinicians; recurrence and skin thinning are recognised issues.

quick.overview:
Keloids are raised scars that grow beyond the original wound. One long-standing medical approach is to inject a corticosteroid such as triamcinolone directly into the scar, sometimes mixed with the chemotherapy drug 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), to reduce its bulk, itch and redness.

It is a clinical procedure, not a cosmetic product. Wikipedia notes that corticosteroid injections were introduced in the mid-1960s and are used within broader treatment plans that may include laser, cryotherapy or surgery.
quick.mechanism: Corticosteroids are described as reducing fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching in the scar tissue. 5-FU is an antimetabolite that is used in combination regimens, including a described 'triple therapy' with pulsed dye laser.
quick.risks: Keloids frequently return after treatment, and Wikipedia reports that surgical removal alone has high recurrence. Intralesional corticosteroids are not recommended in children because of possible growth abnormalities. Rare allergic-type reactions have been reported after keloid injections. Injections are given by clinicians; this article gives no instructions.

lead: Intralesional corticosteroid and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) injection for keloids is a dermatological procedure in which a clinician injects medication directly into a raised keloid scar to flatten it, soften it and reduce symptoms such as itch. For someone whose appearance is affected by a keloid on the ear, jawline, chest, shoulder or back, the aim is a flatter, less conspicuous scar. Triamcinolone acetonide is the corticosteroid most commonly named, and 5-FU is sometimes added or used as an alternative [1][2].

Keloids are benign overgrowths of scar tissue that can extend beyond the boundaries of the original wound, and they can follow acne, piercings, surgery, burns and other skin injuries [1]. Wikipedia describes corticosteroid injection as appearing to reduce fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching, and notes that it is not recommended for children because of possible growth abnormalities. It also describes a combined 'triple therapy' of corticosteroid, 5-FU and pulsed dye laser, said to enhance results and reduce side effects [1]. The American Academy of Dermatology says 50 to 80 percent of keloids shrink after steroid injection but many regrow within five years, which is why dermatologists often combine injections with other treatments [2].

Published comparative evidence is limited. A 2019 randomised trial in Finland compared the two drugs head to head, and several small registered trials have compared triamcinolone alone with combinations or alternatives such as metformin, bleomycin, botulinum toxin and laser-assisted delivery [3][8][9][10][11]. In looksmaxxing communities the topic appears mainly as a medical option for visible scars rather than a self-administered practice.

50-80% of keloids shrink after steroid injection; many regrow within five years (AAD) [2]
Triamcinolone and 5-FU are prescription drugs in the US, UK, Canada and Australia [4][5]

paras: A keloid is a firm, raised scar that grows past the edges of the original injury and can be itchy or painful. Wikipedia lists burns, acne, chickenpox scars, ear piercings, surgical incisions, vaccination sites and tattoos among the injuries that can trigger one, and notes that keloids are most common in people aged 10 to 30 and in people of sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latin American ancestry, with about one-third of people with keloids having an affected first-degree relative [1]. Common sites include the earlobes, chest, shoulders, back and the area over the collarbone [1].

Treatment is usually multimodal, and Wikipedia lists corticosteroid injection, cryotherapy, laser, pressure therapy, silicone sheeting, radiation and surgery among the options [1]. The American Academy of Dermatology says dermatologists often combine treatments because keloids are hard to remove and often return, and that using two or more types of treatment often improves results [2].

Intralesional corticosteroid injection places the drug within the scar tissue itself. Triamcinolone acetonide, sold under brand names including Kenalog, is a synthetic glucocorticoid whose uses include intralesional injection for skin conditions such as hypertrophic scars and keloids [5]. 5-FU is a cytotoxic antimetabolite first used as a cancer chemotherapy in the early 1960s and also used topically for actinic keratosis and warts; its use in keloids is as an off-label injection and is described as part of combination approaches [1][4].

Wikipedia traces intralesional corticosteroid injection for keloids and hypertrophic scars to the mid-1960s, pressure therapy to the 1970s and silicone gel sheeting to the early 1980s [1]. The word keloid comes from the Greek for crab pincers, and in the nineteenth century the condition was called the 'keloid of Alibert' [1].

5-FU was synthesised in the 1950s at Hoffmann-La Roche at the request of Charles Heidelberger, was patented in 1956 and came into medical use in 1962 [4]. A 2019 trial summary describes triamcinolone as the established first-line injection treatment since the 1970s and 5-FU as experimental for keloids at the time [3].

sections.h: What a course of treatment involves
paras: In general terms, the American Academy of Dermatology says patients usually receive a series of injections, with the first ones tending to ease symptoms and soften the scar, and that injections may be followed by surgery or a pressure garment. Before surgery, it says, injections may be given every two to three weeks for four sessions [2]. The injections are given by a dermatologist or surgeon; this article gives no dosing or technique.

Wikipedia reports that surgical excision alone has a recurrence rate of 70 to 100 percent and can produce larger lesions, while combining surgery with radiation, pressure or laser substantially lowers recurrence [1]. The American Academy of Dermatology likewise says recurrence follows surgery alone in nearly all keloids, and that pressure earrings, dressings or garments, worn for many hours a day over several months, can reduce recurrence [2]. Silicone gel sheets, cryosurgery and superficial radiation after surgery are other options it lists [2].

A 2021 review in the International Journal of Dermatology consolidated narrative reviews, systematic reviews and meta-analyses and concluded that keloid management remains multimodal, that no gold-standard treatment provides a consistently low recurrence rate, and that combinations such as laser with intralesional steroid, or 5-FU with steroid, were showing favourable results [14].

Hietanen and colleagues reported a single-blinded randomised trial in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery (2019) of 43 patients with 50 keloids, randomised to intralesional 5-FU or triamcinolone. Remission at six months was 46 percent with 5-FU and 60 percent with triamcinolone, a difference that was not statistically significant, and about half of keloids in each group did not respond. Skin atrophy occurred in 44 percent of the triamcinolone group versus 8 percent of the 5-FU group, and telangiectasia in 50 percent versus 21 percent; hyperpigmentation was seen in three 5-FU patients [3].

Wikipedia notes that a 2022 Cochrane review of silicone gel sheeting compared it with triamcinolone injections among other options but found only two small studies totalling 36 participants, so it could not determine which treatment performs best, and that a Cochrane review of laser therapy found insufficient evidence to compare it with other treatments [1].

Wikipedia notes corticosteroid injection is not recommended in children because of possible growth abnormalities, and that radiotherapy and antimetabolites are likewise not recommended for them [1]. The American Academy of Dermatology says injections can cause lighter spots on darker skin tones, and that other medications can be used to avoid this [2]. In the 2019 randomised trial, triamcinolone was associated with more local skin atrophy and telangiectasia than 5-FU, while 5-FU caused immediate local blistering in one patient and hyperpigmentation in three [3].

A French case report described a patient who developed a Hoigne's syndrome reaction, with fear of dying, after an intra-keloid injection of triamcinolone acetonide with lidocaine [6]. 5-FU given systemically as chemotherapy has a broader side-effect profile, including nausea, bone-marrow suppression and rare cardiotoxicity, and it may harm a fetus; Wikipedia notes that EU and UK labeling since 2020 contraindicates it in people with complete absence of DPD enzyme activity [4].

Registered studies of keloid injection treatments include a phase 3 trial of intralesional treatments (NCT06729840, 45 participants, recruiting) [7], a small comparison of post-surgical injection with triamcinolone versus triamcinolone plus fluorouracil (NCT04710719, 7 participants, completed) [8], a phase 2 comparison of intralesional metformin with triamcinolone (NCT07922616, 30 participants, completed) [9], a trial of bleomycin jet injections (NCT04582305, 14 participants) [10], a study of botulinum toxin to prevent keloid recurrence (NCT05072821, 28 participants) [11], a trial of thermo-mechanical fractional ablation to aid triamcinolone delivery (NCT04597060, 25 participants) [12], and a comparison of corticosteroid injection alone versus combined with Nd:YAG or erbium laser (NCT07263100, 20 participants) [13]. Results are not summarised in the registry entries available to this wiki, and the enrolments are small.

Keloid injections are generally discussed as a clinician-delivered treatment for visible scarring, for example on the ear or face, within hardmaxxing-style conversations about improving appearance through medical procedures. Bodybuilding forum posts show a different side: T Nation users who describe being prone to keloids on the back and shoulders ask how to manage the effect of periodic steroid injections on training and body composition, according to the thread excerpts available [15][16].

Separately, looksmax.org threads discuss triamcinolone acetonide in connection with nose thinning, a use unrelated to keloid treatment; the posts reviewed present it as experimental and carry no clinical data [17]. This article does not cover that use.

timeline.event: 5-FU is patented, following synthesis at Hoffmann-La Roche in the 1950s.[4]
Intralesional corticosteroid injections introduced for keloids and hypertrophic scars.[1]
5-FU comes into medical use as a cancer chemotherapy.[4]
Pressure therapy begins to be used for scars; triamcinolone injection becomes the established first-line injection treatment.[1][3]
Finnish randomised trial compares intralesional 5-FU with triamcinolone in 43 patients.[3]
International Journal of Dermatology review of keloid therapeutic management published.[14]
Cochrane reviews of silicone sheeting and laser therapy find limited evidence for comparing treatments.[1]

lore.intro: Keloid injection is discussed mainly as a standard dermatology procedure; the claims below compare what clinicians and trials report with what patients and community members say.

claims.believers: Patients and clinicians describe injections as the standard first step, and a bodybuilding forum poster says the injections help reduce his scars even though he dislikes the systemic trade-offs.[16]
claims.experts: The American Academy of Dermatology says 50 to 80 percent of keloids shrink after injection, but many regrow within five years.[2]

claims.claim: Adding 5-FU makes injections work better or cause fewer side effects.
claims.believers: Wikipedia describes triple therapy with corticosteroid, 5-FU and pulsed dye laser as reported in adults to enhance results and reduce side effects.[1]
claims.experts: In a 2019 randomised trial, 5-FU and triamcinolone had similar six-month remission (46 vs 60 percent, not significant) with less skin atrophy on 5-FU; a registered trial of 7 participants compared the combination with triamcinolone alone.[3][8]

claims.believers: Some patients report lasting flattening after a course of injections.
claims.experts: The 2021 review says no treatment gives a consistently low recurrence rate, and the AAD says most patients combine injections with other treatments.[14][2]

claims.claim: Corticosteroid injection can thin or lighten skin around the scar.
claims.believers: Patients on bodybuilding forums describe weighing injections against effects on their physiques and skin.[15][16]
claims.experts: Skin atrophy, telangiectasia and lighter spots on darker skin have been reported after intralesional triamcinolone, with atrophy in 44 percent of triamcinolone-treated keloids in one trial.[2][3]

claims.believers: Looksmax.org posters describe triamcinolone, and hydrocortisone as a milder alternative, as a way to reduce nasal swelling, and label their posts experimental.[17]
claims.experts: No study tests triamcinolone for nose appearance; its documented uses include intralesional keloid treatment and other inflammatory skin conditions.[5]
